utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to one and all. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to ask Mr. Mundis to introduce his co-Prosecutor that I see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution today Ken Scott, Daryl Mundis, Roeland Bos and our case manager Skye Winner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I'm not going to ask the Defence counsel teams to present themselves because they're the same people. I should like to say good morning to everyone present in the courtroom; the accused whom we haven't seen for more than a week. I'd also like to say good morning to the representatives of the Prosecution, all the counsel, and everybody else, all the staff in the courtroom. As we're in open session, I can tell you that we weren't here last week because we were on location last week, and we visited most of the sites mentioned in the indictment, and so that having been done, we're going to take up our work again. We didn't sit yesterday because we had a procedural problem, and as the Prosecution asked the witness to present a communication -- to disclose his personal notes, this is something that the witness did, and so the Defence counsel rightly asked that a translation of these papers be seen to, which means that today and tomorrow we're going to have the examination-in-chief of this witness, and the cross-examination will take place sometime later on, and we're going to set a date for that in due course. Without further ado, that is what our proceedings are going to look like today and tomorrow. Mr. Coric isn't here. As you know -- and may I go into private session to explain this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to towards the Prosecution in open session. We're going to have a witness, and you would like to introduce a certain number of documents through that witness. I assume that those documents will be presented in the order that we have received them here, that I have before me. How are you going to proceed? Because as far as I understand it, there are 350 documents. We're going to have to go through them very quickly and demonstrate our professionalism so that we don't waste any time. And if you have envisaged six hours for your examination-in-chief, will that be enough for you to present the documents very quickly and then look at one document, go on to the next, and so on until you've got through the lot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, as I indicated earlier this morning, there are six bundles of documents the Chamber has been provided with. Those six bundles actually fall into two categories. There is one category of documents that is marked "Exhibits for Prosecution witness Christopher Beese." That is one bundle of documents and that is the one that contains the typewritten version of the diary. These are, in effect, the core documents that we will be discussing with this witness more extensively. The remaining five bundles of documents are all ECMM exhibits. There are 384 of them in 5 bundles, and there should also be a landscape version spreadsheet that lists those 384 documents in those five binders that don't have a cover spreadsheet on them. With respect to those documents, Mr. President, we will be laying some foundational questions. The witness himself has gone through those five bundles, or in case, when we dealt with him, in binders. He has reviewed all of those documents. We expect his testimony to be that those are all ECMM reports. He will testify at length. We'll examine him on how ECMM was structured, what its purpose was, how it reported, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is not our intention to take that witness through those 384 ECMM documents. We will take him through the approximately 40 documents in the binder that has the spreadsheet with his name on it, but we will be seeking to tender all six of these bundles of documents into evidence at the conclusion of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just to summarise: You're going to proceed in two ways. You have these documents here in the first binder, and they begin with 1215, et cetera, and then the famous document of 127 pages. You're going to present that, too, and we're going to have very precise questions on that document. And you have other documents, another set of documents which are the ECMM documents, exhibits, and you're going to confirm that they come from the organisation that the witness worked for and that he is aware and knows about the documents, is familiar with them. So during the examination, whether in chief or cross-examination, you are free to ask questions on all these documents. I think that's an intelligent way of proceeding. And without further ado, we're going to have the witness introduced now. Mr. Registrar -- Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, just very briefly with respect to the presentation and tendering of documents, perhaps we ought to exercise caution. We have not been through the documents in detail because we don't know which witnesses are going to come, but in the bundle introduced through Witness Beese there is a large number of documents which were created, compiled by other observers, other ECMM observers, and those observers are planned to appear -- at least, some of them are planned to appear but I don't know which ones. Perhaps we could hear about that so that those documents could go with the other observers to come. But as I have already taken the floor, Your Honour, may I today receive from you, or tomorrow -- rather, may I be accorded three minutes for a request I have to make and a matter I wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what it's about: It's the problem of using PCs, personal computers, by my client in the Detention Unit. According to the rules of the Registry and the detailed rules of the Detention Unit, it is provided for that the accused have access to personal computers. However, a problem has arisen because the administrative rules and the capacity for PCs, installing PCs in the detention centre which the accused can use allows for a maximum of 75 gigabyte capacity whereas my client has his own data and PC with the search engine and everything else which would require 150 gigabytes in total, which means double the power that is provided for according to the rules. So physically 150 gigabytes cannot be put into the computer. We did provide a solution. We were very patient. We had talks with the accused and representatives of the Registrar, but a solution hasn't been found. We did put forward a proposal, two concrete technically applicable solutions, very simple ones: One is to allow the client to use his own external PC with all his information and search systems inside, and the other possibility would be for him to take in the personal computer that contains all this information. Now, I'd like the Court or the Trial Chamber to issue instructions one way or another because it goes to the detriment of the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Our legal officer has informed me that the matter is being dealt with by the Registrar, but as you know, I also dealt with this question of computers, and I personally, as president of this Trial Chamber in charge of organising the proceedings and work of this Trial Chamber, have apprised the Registrar of the situation and asked him why the accused do not have a PC at their disposal, because the Statute indicates that each accused should have maximum facilities in order to be able to ensure their defence. And the maximum is what I have added. "Maximum," the word "maximum" does not exist in the Statute, but one can understand that all the necessary facilities should be provided. I also indicated in the memo that I sent to the Registrar that I happened to discover that Milosevic, for example, had at his disposal these facilities. So I don't understand why there should be any discrimination between individuals. So I am waiting for an answer to the memo I sent, and you have raised another problem which is the question of the double capacity from 75 gigabytes to 150 gigabytes. So there, too, I am going to raise the problem again in that respect, and once I receive a response, I will indicate it to you. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber, if it can make rulings in certain matters, it does so. So far, I cannot deblock money for such-and-such an operation, nor can I take decisions regarding security issues. So that is how matters stand, but we will look into the matter to see how the rights of the Defence teams are impinged. We'll go into that. But rest assured that we as Judges are always -- always pay great attention to the proceedings and do what we can to resolve situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having said that, I'd like to say good morning to Mr. Beese, who has just arrived. I'm just going to check whether you can understand the proceedings in your own language. If that is the case, then please tell me, please let me know that you can hear me and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. "I can" is your answer. Thank you for that. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell us your name, surname, and date of birth, please, by way of introduction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Beese, and I was born on the 1st of March, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can you tell me now -- you were born where, in what town, what country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In London, England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession at that time present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a director of a security company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, and 1994, what was your function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, I was a security advisor commercially. In 1993, I spent the majority of my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a monitor with the European Community Monitoring Mission; and in 1994 I was working again as a commercial security director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you ever testified before this Tribunal or before any other court about the facts that you could have been a witness to in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I testified on one particular day several years ago in the Dario Kordic case here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have already testified before this Tribunal. I'm now going to ask you to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please be seated. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution to go ahead with the examination-in-chief, I'm going to give you some information as to how the proceedings are going to continue. You are going to testify today and tomorrow. The second stage is the cross-examination, which will take place in due course, because the Defence recently learnt about the existence of a document and have asked for more time to be able to study that document and prepare for the cross-examination. And the Trial Chamber allowed the Defence to do that, so your cross-examination will be held at a later stage. You will be coming back depending on the calendar and when you're able to return in order to answer questions by the Defence counsel and the accused as well. But since you've already testified before this Tribunal in the Kordic case, you know how the proceedings are conducted. You're now going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution, the representatives of Madam Carla Del Ponte. The questions are asked in a non-leading, neutral way, and you will be answering the questions you have been asked. When we come to the cross-examination stage, the questions take a different form and usually your answers will be a yes or a no. The Judges sitting before you - normally there are four of us but there are three Judges sitting before you because the fourth is otherwise engaged - so the three Judges sitting in front you can ask you questions at any point in time during the proceedings. If we ask you a question, it is either to clarify an answer you have already given to either one of the parties or because, in the interests of justice, it seems to us to be important to ask the question we deem necessary. And all of us will have the right to ask you questions later on as well. We shall be working in sessions of one and a half hours with breaks in between, 20-minute breaks, to allow you to have a rest and also for technical reasons. Around about 12.30, we're going to adjourn the meeting for an hour and a half to give you a chance to rest and to give the accused a chance to take a rest. It's the coffee break, and we shall reconvene after this adjournment of an hour and a half and have another three-hour session which will take us up to about 5.00 p.m. If you have -- encounter any difficulties during the examination, please let us know and we will try and find a solution. If you have not understood a question properly, please ask the person to reformulate the question, to ask it again. You are a British citizen, and I'd like to inform you that we're in a sort of common law system, following a common law system here, but your words will be transcribed on the screen in front you. That is the transcript and the record of the proceedings, and everything that is said in court is recorded and comes up on the screen. So in general terms, that is what I wanted to tell you by way of information. You have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth, so you will of course tell us about events as they evolved without mendacity, and any infraction of that can, of course, be punished in the form of contempt of Court. That is what I wanted to say. Without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, and we have until 10.30 before the technical break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Because we speak similar languages, I'm going to ask you to ensure there is always a pause between question and answer so that the testimony can be recorded in the transcript. Mr. Beese, can you please tell us, from the period when you left school, a brief summary of your career.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I left school at the age of 18 and entered the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst. I carried out my basic officer training and regular career course training in war studies. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, how long did those courses last?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Twelve months. I then joined an armoured regiment and completed my special to arm -- armour training, which lasted another six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following completion of that training, where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was posted initially to a training area in Great Britain, and then underwent tours of duty in Northern Ireland and tours to Cyprus and Germany. I then left the army as a regular officer in 1977. Following service with the army, I went into the city of London and was an insurance broker with a Lloyds' company from 1978 to 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may, just an additional question: What was your rank when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lieutenant. In 1992 [sic], I determined to return to military service and joined the Sultan of Oman's land forces in Oman. I entered the army there as a captain, as a training officer, to train Dofari soldiers, that is those from southern Oman, in counter-insurgency techniques and border security. I then spent the next five and a half years with a small team raising a reconnaissance regiment responsible for counter-insurgency and border security. I left the Sultan's forces in 1988, and joined the company that I presently serve with in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, if I could just stop you at this point. On page 21, line 2, the transcript indicates that in 1992 you determined to return to military service. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I apologise: 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the period from 1978 until 1982, while you were employed as an insurance broker, did you have any military obligations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I continued to serve as a regular reserve officer assigned to armoured forces in the UK and Germany, spending the occasional week with the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please then continue where you left off when you joined the security company that you're currently employed by.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I joined the security company was assigned to Mozambique, where I worked on a programme approved by the British and American governments to secure Mozambique's fledging economy following its civil war. It was still a time of civil war, and our responsibility was to train guards to protect sugar refineries, power stations, dams, plantations, railway networks. I left there 18 months later and was reassigned to transportation security in the United Kingdom. There I was responsible for countering the hijack of vehicles by those seeking to secure electronic goods, wine, spirits, tobaccos and other sensitive items. Some 12 months later I was assigned to Heathrow where I was consultant to a support team working with British Airways to adjust their security arm to changing market conditions. In 1992, that contract was completed with British Airways. I did some time in the Congo, some two months as regional manager in lieu of the full time manager, and returned to Britain in the summer of 1992. I then took a gap and later in the year applied to the Foreign Office for work with the European Community in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Mr. Beese, in just a moment, but let me ask you, you told us earlier that during the time you served in the army, you were with an armoured regiment.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that regiment was deployed during the time that you served with that regiment.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I spent time in England with battle tanks, Chieftain battle tanks. I spent time in a dismounted role as an infantryman in Northern Ireland, and exercised as an infantryman in Cyprus and as an armoured regiment in Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, what was the time period that you were in Northern Ireland, and what was the situation like at that time on the ground in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I spent the better part of 1976 in Northern Ireland, at a time when there was an effort by terrorists to kill policemen, and our responsibility at the time was to control the movement of people, vehicles, and to try to prevent further losses of the police. This took me to Belfast and County Antrim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, sir, that your reserve obligations with the British army ended, what was the most senior rank that you had attained in the British army?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the most senior rank that you obtained in the Sultan of Oman's armed forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the situation on the ground when you were in Mozambique, working for the security company that is your employer.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Mozambique was still in a state of civil war between the Marxist government and Renamo guerrillas, backed by a regime in South Africa, who endeavoured to interfere with the economy and normal proceedings in Mozambique. Our responsibility was to try to restore the economy by securing railways, power stations, dams, in support of an effort, I believe, by the United States and Britain to return the country to a degree of normality in pursuit of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Beese, that you were there for approximately 18 months in Mozambique.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period when you were in Mozambique?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Through the most part of 1978 and half of 1979. Wrong. I'm sorry. I say that again. Sorry. For the most part of 1988 and half of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before we took this little digression, Mr. Beese, you were telling us about applying to -- through the Foreign Office, the British Foreign Office, to become an EC monitor. Can you tell us how that process worked. How did you become aware that the Foreign Office was searching for monitors? How did you apply?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I heard from colleagues who had worked out of theatre, by which I mean outside Europe, before, principally those who worked in Oman and Africa, who said that they were enjoying the work in Yugoslavia, it gave them good purpose, it was an opportunity to apply skills they'd learnt elsewhere in terms of border security, mediation, observation. They -- they thought this might well suit me, so I applied to the Foreign Office to see if there was a suitable opportunity in Yugoslavia for my services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the response of the Foreign Office?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The Foreign Office interviewed me, initially said they had no spaces at the time but bore in mind my interest, said it would be some months before I might be called again. In fact, I was called in less than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately what time period were you called back by the Foreign Office? The month and the year, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was called back at the beginning of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened after you received this call from the Foreign Office?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: They interviewed me again, and after interview, gave me notice that I would depart at the beginning of January, 1993; and I flew on the 2nd of January, 1993, to the headquarters of the European Community Monitoring Mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll ask -- I'll ask you a number of questions about the European Community Monitoring Mission in a moment, but can you tell us, after your arrival in Zagreb on 2 January, 1993, how long you remained. How long was your mission in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I continued to serve in Yugoslavia, with the exception of two short periods of leave outside the country, until the 21st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Beese, what steps were undertaken to prepare you for this mission prior, prior to your departure for Zagreb? What steps did you take to prepare yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I had followed the course of the conflict as a normal -- as a normal member of the public, an observer; television coverage principally, newspaper coverage. I understood the general dynamics of the conflict but not necessarily the detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long, sir, were you in Zagreb after your arrival in 2 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I remained in Zagreb, being briefed, while my assignment was determined, and I was finally deployed to Split on the 8th of January, and to Siroki Brijeg on the 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, what types of preparation did you undergo during the period you were in Zagreb from 2 through 8 January, 1993, for your mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We were given technical training on the Capsat communication system and the high frequency radio system, we were given refresher training on first aid, and we were given briefings on the general situation, personalities, places, the layout of the United Nations Protected Areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Beese, you've made reference to the Capsat communication system. Can you tell us a little bit more about Capsat; what it was, how it worked?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The Capsat system is a satellite system designed, I understand, principally for use by fishing fleets, by the Danish manufacturer Thrane and Thrane. It is used to transmit data entered through a PC system - which would be familiar to us as a laptop computer - in a suitcase with a separate transmitter unit and cabling. So generally you would deploy the satellite transmitter outside of a window and type in a report, for instance, save it, and/or transmit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How big was this system?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Small suitcase size. It enabled us to carry it by vehicle, to open it, deploy it, use it from buildings or from a vehicle if necessary. It gave us the means to communicate almost instantly with any other Capsat system across the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time of your arrival and deployment with the European Community Monitoring Mission, or ECMM, can you tell us a little bit about the structure of that entity.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The mission, I understand, was established during the conference at Brioni in 1991 and deployed in July, 1991, sponsored by the European Community and the Conference for Security and Cooperation in Europe. Its aim was to field monitors, people into the former Yugoslavia who could then properly report on the affairs, the practical affairs as they took place in Yugoslavia to the presidency of the European Community and to the peace talks in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the structure or organisation of ECMM on the ground in the former Yugoslavia at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: When I arrived, the headquarters of the ECMM was based in the Hotel I in Zagreb, Croatia. The mission had regional centres then across the constituent parts of the former Yugoslavia and in surrounding territories, though there was a regional centre in Zagreb that cared for matters arising in Croatia. There were regional centres in Hungary, Bulgaria, Macedonia, Albania, and in Belgrade. There had been a regional centre in Mostar, or at least a coordination centre in Mostar and a regional centre in Sarajevo until May, 1992. At that point in time, the conflict became so intense as to require its withdrawal. So as I arrived, the European Mission was moving back into Bosnia-Herzegovina. It did this by establishing a coordination centre in Grude, a second in Tuzla, and a third in Zenica. The regional centres communicated with their monitors through coordination centres which had reporting to them one or more teams of monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, you've mentioned teams. Can you tell us a little bit about what these teams were, how many people they had, and how they were structured?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: A team normally comprised a single vehicle with communication systems, crewed by a driver, a senior monitor, where possible a second monitor, and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To whom did the teams report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The teams reported to the head of the coordination centre. The teams would operate during the day on their given tasks, return to the base in the evening, compile their reports, and produce them for the head of the coordination centre. The teams may or may not be collocated with the coordination centre. For instance, in Herzegovina, when I arrived, the head of coordination centre was in -- was based in Siroki Brijeg with a satellite team in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown a document marked P 09493.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you see a document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Not presently. It's now present on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: This shows the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm sorry, we still don't have the document on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ELMO, please, Mr. Usher. ELMO. May it be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, can you tell us what this document shows, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It shows the outline structure of the European Community Monitoring Mission as it was through 1993, with particular reference to the teams allocated to RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, from that answer that each of the other regional centres would have had similar coordination centres under them but they're not depicted on the chart?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: That might be the case, but they would not have had the strength that's shown here on the RC Zenica organisation because they did not face the complexity of operations that we faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Beese, starting at the bottom of the chart, explain the chart and how it works up to the Zagreb headquarters at the top.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: You can see the layout of teams at the bottom. On the left Mike 1, 2, 3 and 4. Tango 1, Tango 2, and then Victor 1 to 4. Those teams would have reported to their respective coordination centre. The coordination centre would report daily its findings, that is activity in its location, its area of responsibility, and some analysis to the regional centre, in our case to the regional centre in Zenica when it was established. The regional centre would then assess and analyse the information it had been given from the coordination centres and report its findings to Zagreb each evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, can you please explain to us what the Mike, Tango and Victor that you just referred to are abbreviations for.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Because there were numerous name changes in the region at the time I joined it -- some communities had been renamed. For instance, to show you the complexity, I was assigned to CC Grude, which is the coordination centre initially established in Grude, but by the time I joined, it was based in Siroki Brijeg that had recently changed its name from Listica. It was much easier to assign radio call signal to a team than to give it a name. Additionally, in case a team was redeployed to a new area, the team continued to use its call-sign. Much easier to understand who is who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask now that the witness be shown the exhibit that's been marked P 09607.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the number again because what appeared on the screen doesn't seem to be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you see the document on the screen in front you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe this document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The document shows the reporting chain from the field, that is the monitoring teams, all the way through the command structure of the European Community Monitoring Mission into the net users of that information. That is the European Commission, and particularly its presidency, which at the time I arrived had just changed from the British to the Danes, and to the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia conducting peace talks in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you take us on this chart from the bottom to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It shows here how the monitors would tour their area of responsibility, report each day their findings to the coordination centre to which they reported, which in turn would submit a consolidated report to the regional centre. It does show here sometimes where there are communications difficulties or there are special reports a monitoring team could report directly to the regional centre. The regional centre had a larger staff, which included personnel assigned for analysis. The regional centre would be able to produce in the evening a report of activity in its area and transmit it to Zagreb headquarters in the Hotel I. It would additionally send weekly summary reports and, occasionally, special subject reports. The headquarters in Zagreb would analyse the reports from across the region and produce its own summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where would these -- where would these summaries and reports ultimately go?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Physically, most of the reports from the region would sit in the Hotel I in Zagreb. Practically, the information would be distributed to the foreign ministers of the countries contributing to the European Community Monitoring Mission, which were the Member States of the European Community as well as others from the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, which included Canada, Poland, and Slovakia. They, representing their governments, would be able to better understand the circumstances in the region. The information also went to David Owen and Cyrus Vance, and later, Thorvald Stoltenberg in Geneva whose responsibility it was to encourage the parties to conflict towards peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown P 09603.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who produced this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it depicts, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: This was a -- a somewhat quickly produced document. Lacking more sophisticated design software, this is drawn by hand to illustrate the areas of responsibility for each of the teams operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina under command of the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the various markings that are placed in this map covering the regional centre Zenica's area of responsibility, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We show the principal communities and the principal roads. We then show by area of responsibility where each team was principally allocated a responsibility. Therefore, in the south those given a Mike call-sign were assigned to the coordination centre in the Mostar area. At the time, there was a Mike 1, a Mike 2, and then Mike 9 which is the head the coordination centre, so you can take it there were three teams there. I beg your pardon, I see there is also two further more to the north. So there are four Mike teams in operation, and one head of coordination centre. This depicts also the highest level of manning that we had in June and July after reinforcement from other areas. Normally that area would have been covered, as it was when I arrived, by three teams only. This shows four teams plus a fifth coordination team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, for the sake of completeness, can you please move up the map northwards and describe for us what we see in the centre and top parts of this map.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: In the centre the call-signs are Victor call-signs, derived from the Vitez name where they first entered the region. There are a number of teams there and a headquarters team, the head of coordination centre, based in Zenica. In this particular case, the coordination centre was collocated with the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what is the call-sign for the headquarters team that was collocated in Zenica with the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I don't recall that the RC teams had call-signs as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, you misunderstood. The coordination team headquarters that was collocated, what was the call-sign?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Victor 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, can you now move to the northernmost part of the map and describe for us what that indicates.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The Tuzla area produced Tango call-signs. The front lines were relatively stable. It required fewer assets to monitor and, therefore, was confined to two mobile teams and one headquarter team in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The call-sign for the headquarters team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Tango 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, when, approximately, did you produce this map or this sketch?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I would have produced this when I was appointed deputy head of regional centre in Zenica in June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, just in general so that we have an overview of what the teams did, can you tell us what the teams did on a -- on a daily basis? What did they actually do?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The teams would be assigned a set of normal operating tasks, such as routine liaison with civic authorities, routine liaison with government authorities, routine liaison with supporting organisations such as UNPROFOR, UNHCR, ICRC, and the monitoring of any cease-fire. If it was given specific tasking, such as to go and do this or to go and do that, it would do so. Otherwise, it would fall back on its normal tasking, and that was sufficient to enable the teams to roam their areas of responsibility at will and to determine what is actually happening, to produce reports on military, socio-economic, and other activity, and to understand what the leaders in their particular area from whichever denomination they came from, what their views were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were the teams put together?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: There was a continual turnover of monitors. Different countries dispatched their monitors to Yugoslavia for different periods of time. Therefore, one monitor might serve four months, one from another country might serve six months, and some countries, such as Great Britain, were prepared to assign their monitors for up to two years. Therefore, there were some with considerable experience and some with very little. There were also differences in skill base between those assigned to the mission. Some might be armoured officers, some might be intelligence officers. Almost all of them were serving or former officers of their armed forces, and therefore there might be retired officers of the rank of colonel to general, there might be much younger officers in their late 20's, lieutenants, and captains. It would be appropriate to mix the teams, so you mixed the experience in theatre with experience generally of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of clothing did the monitors wear?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We all wore white: White tops - that's shirts, pullovers - and white trousers. We had EC badging, with the normal blue background, yellow stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of vehicles did the teams use?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Two types. There were normal what I would call soft-skinned vehicles available, that is a normal production Land Rover, Nissan Patrol, Toyota Land Cruiser, Mitsubishi Shogun. A four-by-four able to traverse the terrain competently or, in times of difficulty, there were armoured Mercedes Gelandewagens available. They had been contributed by Germany and were vehicles formerly used on the border between West and East Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What types of arms, if any, did the EC monitors carry?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The EC monitors were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago, Mr. Beese, as reflected on line 17 of page 34, that some of the monitors might be armoured officers, some might be intelligence officers. What role, if any, were the EC monitors playing in terms of intelligence gathering?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The need was for information rather than intelligence. Intelligence is a sensitive word and it was imperative that the EC mission was seen to be a provider of relevant information as opposed to military disposition. It was important that the EC monitors were not seen to be spies, that they were not seen to pass military dispositions between the various parties they met and discuss matters with, and that sensitive military information was not generally available over Capsat or any other record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate for us on the difference between information and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The questions we asked of the people we met, whether they were civil leaders, politicians, or military, was what are their feelings about the current situation? What intentions did they have, if any? The various parties to the conflict would have a public intention, such as to -- to work closely with another party towards peace. It was not necessary then to ask them for details of military dispositions but to pass -- pass on information regarding their -- their search for peace. They had the opportunity to speak frankly, we had the opportunity to report accurately. On occasion, it was quite clear to us that activity in practice did not match declared intention, and there -- possibly there might be a conflict between the provision of information or intelligence, but actually the requirement was to corroborate the main aim and the declared intention, or to question it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, in what way, if any, was information shared by ECMM with the various parties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: ECMM would not share the intentions or declarations of one party to another except where it was explicitly understood that that would be the case. The ECMM itself as an organisation would share its information with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago, Mr. Beese, that there were also liaison functions between ECMM and other international agencies.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did those liaison functions work on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Very informally. The international agencies themselves struggled to provide the assets and resource necessary to maintain a presence across the area. Therefore, in Mostar there might be a UNHCR office, it might concentrate principally on humanitarian aid or on protection matters such as the protection of refugees. They would not be present in every town. ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, likewise had scarce resource. They needed sufficient to monitor human interest, and it was for the teams to know who the representatives were in each area, of those international organisations, and to communicate with them, work with them where possible, and to be mutually supporting where relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How would you differentiate or distinguish between the role of the ECMM and the role, for example, of UNPROFOR at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: UNPROFOR had a very clearly defined mission, and in that context it was closely -- working closely with UNHCR principally for the delivery of aid. The ECMM had a much broader mandate, and whereas United Nations units necessarily reported through a strict control mechanism and it would have been inappropriate for military personnel within the United Nations to deal with people of a different standing in their region, EC monitors were individuals able to communicate with whomever they wished, and to travel to see whomever they wished at any time. They had much greater flexibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how did this greater flexibility manifest itself on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The connection between command and control and troops on the ground could be worked more efficiently if, for instance, a team could monitor a cease-fire and compliance with a government directive. And I might give an example. In Gornji Vakuf, the team would liaise with the troops either engaged in conflict with another faction or withdrawing and be able to speak, if there was any difficulty, with the command and control structure or even the politicians in Mostar to see -- to check whether instructions were being complied with. It would have been very difficult for United Nations observers to work with both troops on the ground and politicians in a government building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, Mr. Beese, what were the main, if you will, modes of action that the monitors undertook?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: On my arrival, the concern was the free flow of humanitarian aid. So there was a concentration on the mechanisms by which humanitarian aid moved from the coast to the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were also issues of tension between particularly the three parties to the conflict, that is two working together, the Croats and the Muslims, and their common adversary the Serb. Those were the principal activities; humanitarian aid and tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the role of ECMM with respect to humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The ECMM had a common interest in ensuring a constant flow of humanitarian aid, both for humanitarian reasons and because any obstruction to aid would inevitably create tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But what precisely -- what was the more precise role? Was ECMM actually accompanying convoys or assisting with humanitarian relief? Can you be a little bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The ECMM monitored the movement of convoys, generally speaking. It was not a question of how many trucks and how many days, but whether aid was free flowing or not. If it was hindered, that was a matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the primary way in which ECMM looked after issues of tension between the parties at the time of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: ECMM had the option to address a matter locally or centrally. Therefore, a team would endeavour to manage tension locally with local commanders. If that failed, the team would refer the matter to the coordination centre. In Herzegovina, for instance, the coordination centre had the opportunity to meet with senior officials of the HVO in Mostar. If it was believed that the matter was so serious it was beyond the means of the coordination centre to resolve, it would report the matter to the regional centre, at that time based in Split prior to its deployment to Zenica, and the regional centre, headed by a diplomat, usually an active ambassador, would have the opportunity to address the government of whichever party directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This would be an appropriate place for the first technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to reconvene at approximately ten to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's continue until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now like to turn your attention to your departure from Zagreb. Can you tell us -- you told us earlier that you arrived in Siroki Brijeg on about the 9th of January, 1993. Did you make any intermediate stops in travelling from Zagreb to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was initially sent from Split by vehicle -- sorry, from Zagreb by vehicle to Split, where I spent two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you do in Split during those two days?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Briefed on the local circumstance of operations to the north and east of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention now, sir, to your arrival in Siroki Brijeg. Can you tell us what further preparation, if any, you made upon your arrival in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane, the Irish head of coordination centre, briefed me on what his teams were doing in the Mostar region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time of your arrival, sir, where was -- just so we're all clear, where was the coordination centre headquarters at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The headquarters was based in a private house in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time of your arrival on 9 January, 1993, how many teams reported to the coordination centre headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Three. One was based in Tomislavgrad and lived there; two teams were based out of Siroki Brijeg, including that of Ray Lane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what team you were initially assigned to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was assigned to the second team working out of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were the other members of that team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Variously, I would accompany Juan Valentin, a Spanish officer, or Volmer Svensen, a Danish officer, or Ray Lane himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time of your arrival, sir, how many monitors were assigned to the coordination centre headquartered in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many support personnel were assigned to the coordination centre headquartered in Siroki Brijeg upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We had no core staff. There were only the four monitors and two drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What assets were available to you in terms of interpretation or translation support?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We could make use of local interpreters as they were available. Other than that, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the approximate date when you were sent out on your first mission with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I started moving out around the area, both to familiarise myself and engage in normal tasking business, on the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm simply calling to the attention of the Trial Chamber and to the Defence that the witness does seem to have a piece of paper in front of him, which I wanted to do just in terms of transparency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, can you tell us what this piece of paper is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It is a list of key events or key dates to remind me of dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you put that in your pocket. Please continue. If at a certain point in time you forget something and you would like to refresh your memory, please tell us. Otherwise, try and answer the questions as they have been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you recall the approximate mission or mandate that you were given for that first mission that you were sent out with as an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We were looking at the movement of aid from Metkovic towards Mostar, and we were examining the circumstances of refugees, mostly Muslim refugees, living in Southern Herzegovina, or small pockets of Serb citizens who remained in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you undertake this specific mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Excuse me, is that for the day or for the period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, for that -- for that -- I guess you answered that question; that was a one-day mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. But it was consistent with the work of those days, for a week or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately -- again, in this period I'd like to focus on January, 1993, for the moment. During the period January, 1993, approximately how many days a week were you out on mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Almost every day, though Sunday was inevitably a quieter day because there were fewer officials to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, in January, 1993, if it's possible, can you describe for us a typical day as an ECMM monitor based out of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The team would depart the base at around 8.00 in the morning, would travel to one of the -- one of the towns in the area, for instance, Ljubuski to visit refugees, to Glusci to visit a Serb pocket, to Stolac to visit the hospital and the community there, to Mostar to liaise with ministers and HVO and Muslim officials responsible for humanitarian aid such that we came to understand what was working and possibly what wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would you do after you went to these locations or met with the people that you were liaising with? What would you do then?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Towards the end of the day we would return to the base, we would then report to Ray Lane, either with a verbal briefing or with a short written report, to enable him to understand what we had found, to discuss matters of mutual interest. He likewise would brief us on what he'd been doing, and by the end of the day we would understand, hopefully, what was happening in our area and be in a position to brief Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, just so that we're clear, sir, how was this briefing to Zagreb undertaken?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane would produce a report and transmit it by Capsat through the regional centre in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, other than monitoring humanitarian missions or humanitarian aid relief, what other missions you were assigned to undertake as an ECMM monitor in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Where there were issues of tension, we were required either to report it if it was new or to react to it if it was known. Therefore, for instance, as we became more familiar as part of the move of the mission back into Bosnia, we were reacquainted with the officials of the various parties, and there were only two parties of significance in the Mostar area, and that is the HVO with its political and military apparatus, and the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again in this period January, 1993, do you recall some of the, as you put it, parties of significance in the Mostar area? Who were the people that you were actually speaking with or liaising with in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We had access to HVO officials of various levels responsible for humanitarian aid, for matters of defence, military matters, and political. We had access to the armija officers, either at brigade level or later at corps level. Therefore, we dealt with the likes of Arif Pasalic on one hand and the likes of Bruno Stojic and his assistant Slobodan Bozic on the other hand. We also dealt with the minister -- HVO minister responsible for humanitarian affairs, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific meetings with any of these individuals that occurred in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Apart from routine discussions, the discussion perhaps of most significance was with the brigade commander of the armija in Mostar who briefed us on an ultimatum that had been given the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the HVO to disband and to come under control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you recall the name of this brigade commander of the armija in Mostar who briefed you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific time line or time period when this ultimatum was given and when it was set to expire?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane first heard of the ultimatum when he met the brigade commander on the 15th. The brigade commander stated that tension was increasing, that Muslim people were being arrested, and that the HVO had announced by public means, by word of mouth, by radio broadcast, but not through the armija, that the armija was to come under command of the HVO with effect from the 20th. That was not expected to be a smooth transfer of authority. It was expected to be resisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Beese, for the purpose of the transcript, when you make reference to the 15th and the 20th, can you tell us the month and year those dates refer to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We became aware of the -- of the ultimatum on the 15th when Ray Lane met with the brigade commander. He understood there were tensions and that the ultimatum was due to come into effect on the 20th of January. I then went to meet with the brigade commander again on the 16th of January, following Ray Lane's visit, and was given specific details of the ultimatum, such as the date of implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, sir, what the conditions were like in Mostar during this period 15, 16 January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Mostar was a tense city. Mostar was subject to periodic shelling by Serbs. Serbian artillery was based on Mount Velez, immediately to the east of Mostar. The Serbs would shell the city with four, six, a dozen shells a day or every other day. That was the principal cause of -- of tension, though there was increasing tension between the HVO and the armija, between the two communities. The HVO had established checkpoints around the city of Mostar, and it was necessary even by that stage for Muslim commanders - I can't say what it was like for the private citizen - to seek permission from the HVO to leave or enter Mostar. The HVO appeared to have control of much of Mostar and its daily life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you obtained this information from this ABiH brigade commander, what did you do with that information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The information was deemed to be so serious and potentially so destabilising that it was necessary for my team to travel immediately to Split where Ray Lane was discussing the matter with the head of the regional centre, Ambassador Beaussou, and to report to them directly what I'd heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that briefing with Ambassador Beaussou.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane understood the implications, as did the ambassador. The ambassador reported the matter to Zagreb and determined to approach senior officials in the HVO to determine whether this was in fact true and what it meant, and therefore the ambassador travelled back to Mostar on the 19th to meet with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, at any point between your meeting on the 16th and the 19th of January, 1993, if you were again in the immediate area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. It became our -- our responsibility then to monitor tension, to monitor what was to be a curfew imposed by the HVO, and to respond if in fact the ultimatum gave rise to HVO action in an attempt to enforce the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what was the geographic scope of the curfew to be imposed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I understood it was -- it was a general curfew applying to the region, though in practice with a relatively small Muslim population and community spread amongst the towns of Herzegovina, those of Grude, Posusje, Ljubuski, Capljina and Citluk, the curfew really was imposed on Mostar and not on the outlying towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any discussions that you had with ABiH officials during this time period from the 16th -- again not talking about your discussion with the brigade commander but after that meeting with the brigade commander up until the 19th? Did you have any further discussions with any ABiH officials?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We began to talk then with the corps commander Arif Pasalic, but I can't recall the date specifically without reference to my account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But it was between the 16th and the 19th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics of what Arif Pasalic told you during that time period?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Arif Pasalic related in greater detail the restrictions imposed on them by the HVO. He recounted how his headquarters had been cut off telephonically, how power and water supplies might be interrupted, and life generally made more difficult. He also related how he had very few troops of his own in Mostar because the majority of armija troops were based on the front line to the east, in confrontation with the Serbs. Therefore, the HVO had many more troops in and around Mostar than he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now, Mr. Beese, to that meeting of the 19th of January, 1993. Do you recall who was in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was not present, but I am aware that Ray Lane accompanied Ambassador Beaussou to meetings with Mr. Prlic. Also, I believe with Mr. -- with General Petkovic. And it was through General Petkovic that the word of concern - for that was what the European Community expressed - concern that at this particular stage implementation of the ultimatum would do no good to the general peace process at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you briefed on what occurred at this meeting after its conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Immediately afterwards by Ray Lane when he returned to the coordination centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did he tell you took place at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: He related how the HVO had heard the EC expression of concern and how the HVO regarded the transfer of responsibility for all forces to the HVO as a natural progression of organisation in the area. It would not be unusual for Mr. Prlic to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour, at this point. Please withhold finishing that sentence. At this point now the gentleman is commenting about a meeting that he wasn't present at and now he's about to voice an opinion. So if some foundational background can be put in for the gentleman to voice an opinion, that's fine, but since he wasn't present, I find it offensive that we would have a witness here testifying to matters that are clearly, you know, outside his knowledge. It's clear hearsay, and I understand hearsay can come in. I don't have a problem with that. He was briefed, but he wasn't present. So now he's going into a mindset of someone who was at a meeting where he wasn't present, and that I do object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, the Judges and the Chamber are trying to follow the logic of that. A moment ago, you told us that in chapter 13 there were personal opinions of the witness expressed -- or, rather, chapter 13 wasn't there and you wanted to know them. Now he wants to give an opinion and you are opposed to it. Now, I'm doing my best as a Cartesian to find my way around all that. Could you enlighten me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll help you out, Your Honour, I'll help you out. I haven't seen his reflections, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, help me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will. I don't have his chapter on reflections and I don't know what's in it and how he arrives at certain conclusions or reflections, but in this particular instance he's saying -- or he began by saying it would not be unusual -- I cut him off at that point. In this particular instance, he wasn't present at the meeting. He gets a briefing according to his own testimony, and now he is going to comment about a -- about somebody's mindset at a briefing where he wasn't present. Now, if he has met Mr. Prlic and a question can be posed to the gentleman after meeting with Mr. Prlic what his impressions are of Mr. Prlic, and so on and so forth; I don't have a problem. But keeping in mind that this is a purely hearsay testimony, I do have some concerns, and I think that I need to highlight it so at least it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Mr. Mundis, don't ask the witness about a meeting that he didn't attend and ask him his impressions. There are other subjects where the witness was present and that would be far more useful. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, during the time period that you were in Bosnia from January through July, 1993, did you ever have occasion to meet with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On approximately how many occasions during that six- or seven-month period did you meet with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Perhaps eight occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sitting here today, are there any themes that were consistently told to you or expressed to you by Mr. Prlic during these approximately eight meetings that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prlic, as was representative of the line given us by he and his colleagues, was that the HVO represented the only organised entity in the region and, therefore, whether the issue in hand was a matter of humanitarian aid or military operation or internal affairs, matters of education, culture, licensing and the like, the HVO represented the best option, indeed the only option, for running the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return now to the briefing that you received by Mr. Lane following the meeting on the 19th of January, 1993. Do you recall any of the specifics of what Mr. Lane told you had taken place at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I don't mean to -- I hate to do this. I understand that we have -- that hearsay can come in. If Mr. Lane is on the witness list, he is obviously the best evidence for this sort of testimony, and that would trump hearsay testimony, as I understand how the rules are and how they should be applied. So if Mr. Lane is going to be coming in to talk about a meeting that he had with Mr. Prlic, I think it's wiser to have Mr. Lane describe this as opposed to this gentleman who, after all, got a briefing, keeping in mind that hearsay does come in, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, if Mr. Lane is on the witness list and is coming in, then you can ask Mr. Lane directly rather than asking the witness about hearsay evidence. And he can go back to what the man told him but with less precision. So are you going to have Mr. Lane come in to testify? And if so, you can ask him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could respond to that. Again, I think, as Mr. Karnavas recognised several times, hearsay evidence is admissible. Whether Mr. Lane comes and testifies or not, if Mr. Lane were to come six months from now and say immediately after the meeting I briefed Mr. Beese, then I'm open to criticism as to why I didn't ask Mr. Beese about the contemporaneous briefing that Mr. Lane gave to him. What we're trying to simply do is to say, in effect, whether we call Mr. Lane or not, if Mr. Lane's recollection of that meeting is corroborated by what this witness tells us he was told on the very day that that meeting took place, that's another reason for why this type of evidence should be admissible. It's simply a question of weight at the end of the day anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Judges agree. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Beese, can you recall any of the specifics of what Mr. Lane briefed you on following this meeting on the 19th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I'd rather refer to my account in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, many details -- many events took place in that time. It is now some time ago. From events one distilled a view of various processes. It is much easier for me to recall the processes and the themes than it is some of the specifics without me relating to my notes. And when it comes to detail, I would rather confine myself to what I can accurately recall through my account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, with the Trial Chamber's leave, let me digress at this point and ask the witness some foundational questions with respect to his account, as he's called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you made reference to your account. Can you tell us, please, what you're referring to when you say "my account."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: When I returned from the former Yugoslavia, I inevitably had many concerns in my head. I had a need to put down in writing what I had experienced, both for the benefit of my family, so they would understand what it was that I'd been and done, perhaps with a view also to improving the training for monitors in future missions. I therefore put down in 1994 and late 1993, when I returned from the mission, as much detail as I could, adding to it a certain amount of personal feelings as experienced by a monitor to show the personal conflicts and issues that a monitor encounters. The account was not meant to be a detailed record of everything that was said and done. It does include a certain amount of detail, and where I have written detail and comment on people's comments, that is, to my understanding, accurate. I produced this account from records I had, from notebooks and recollections, but it was not at all meant to be a diary of events other than the fact that it was a process, something that took place over several months, and is therefore my product and my product only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, at this point I understand -- I don't want to interrupt again, but if we're going to be using this as a basis, as a foundation to get this account in so the gentleman can use to refresh his memory, what I -- I would be asking for all of the records and all of the notebooks upon which this account was based on, because I think they are part and parcel. They all come in as one package. So I want to make this objection right on -- on -- right up front at this point. Before there's an introduction of this account, I would like to have a commitment that we're going to be getting the records and notebooks upon which this account was drafted and whether those exist and what have you. I think it's fair. It all comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can you ask the witness questions as to how he was able to do this, how -- whether he was helped by anybody, before presenting him with a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If not, then I'll be asking the questions myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me return, Mr. President, to the witness's previous answer and we'll build on it from there, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you told us that you produced this account from - and this is on line 7 of page 53 - from records that you had, from notebooks and recollections. Can you tell us, sir, the process by which you created these earlier notebooks and/or recollections. How did you do this? How did you accumulate the information in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this is -- well, I object to the form of the question. We can ask where do they come from, where do these notebooks come from, the recollections and the records. I would -- it's a much cleaner way of asking the question, because the other one is somewhat suggestive that they were actually made in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to intervene at this point. Sir, it would appear that you produced a document on your recollections of your mission. You explained a moment ago that it was for your family, perhaps for history, or whatever. Now, that document, where did you produce it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
