utterances.text: Your Honour, I produced it on a computer after hours at my place of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And could you tell us what month that was? You said the end of 1993, beginning of 1994. Could you be more precise and perhaps give us a month? Because as far as I understood it, you left Bosnia-Herzegovina in July. So several months elapsed. And when did you take up this work, as of what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I began in December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So produced it with your -- on your computer, based on your memory, and as Mr. Karnavas suggested, you used other documents, other paper. So did you do it on the basis of other elements that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, through my time in Yugoslavia, I maintained a normal pocket diary which, for instance, gave me the locations I was in day by day and something of what took place. I also had notebooks wherein I recorded some of the substance of meetings that I attended. I also had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So I have discovered that you had a normal pocket diary and notebooks. Is that right? And where is that pocket diary and the notebooks? Where are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a -- a copy of my diary, and I have the notebooks in my hotel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you not provide all this material to the Prosecutor? Because apparently what you did supply them with was a document of 127 pages but not the rest of the material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the notebooks make sense to me as the writer of those notebooks, but the notes themselves do not necessarily on their own make sense to other people. A single word on a particular page might remind me specifically of something that was said but might make no sense to another reader. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document that you did provide the Prosecution with, as far as you are concerned, is the faithful original of the diary that you were keeping and the notebooks in which you made your little entries. Could I understand it that way? That it is the transcription and faithful transcribing of what you had jotted down in your pocket diary or in your other notes or notebooks, your little memo pads or whatever you used. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- it is a distillation. It doesn't contain, of course, every word or every remark in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we can observe that it was a selection, a distillation, as you say. Counsel Karnavas, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can only speak from my own experience of having received reports, for instance, from police officers where they're based on notes that they take in the field, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that in my experience sometimes there are sometimes minor, sometimes major inconsistencies from the notes to what is actually put in the report where the report is written after, once they get into the field. I think it's discoverable. I don't think we can just take the account without taking the notebooks. So I certainly would -- I am moving, making an oral application at this point in time, for everything. And again, there is a mechanism, there is a mechanism -- I'll wait. If I could be heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we understand. We're trying to save time here. Counsel Karnavas, the witness has taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth and the whole truth. That obliges him to tell us exactly what he noticed and what he was able to write down. Now, you would like him to bring in piles and piles of documents to test that. That would take years. We have to get to the core of the matter quickly, and the heart of the matter is this famous document that we were referring to a moment ago. During the cross-examination, you will have ample opportunity to answer him -- to ask him any questions that you deem necessary and that concern your client. So as we go along, we will see whether there is any need to complete what he says with respect to the documents that he has in his hotel room. We'll see that in due course. But we don't want to waste any more time and waste these proceedings dealing with a problem which is losing time and is not advancing our search for the truth. So let's hear what the witness is going to tell us about the events he attended. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I believe we were at the point where the witness indicated that he needed to refer to the account, as he's put it, in order to answer the question I'd asked him, so at this point in time, rather than using the e-court system, I'm proposing that the witness be provided with a bound copy of the account which we've marked as P 09601.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Beese, the question that was put to you several minutes ago was whether you had any recollections of what Ray Lane briefed you on immediately after the meeting of 19 January, 1993. Mr. Beese, if you could look at paragraph 68, I believe.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It is apparent to me here that the meeting between the ambassador and Mr. Prlic was a little one-sided inasmuch as it was the EC who wished to deliver a message to the HVO, and therefore it does not give comment on the HVO response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, Mr. President, I'd ask the witness be shown P 01215.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could just now close the account but perhaps leave it to the side. Mr. Beese, do you see a document before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that document is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The document I have before me is in -- written in Croatian, I believe, and although I have an idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. We need to get the witness to be able to see the English version of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I can see a report written by the head of regional centre in Split to the headquarters of the ECMM in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there, sir. You said you saw the report was written by the head of the regional centre in Split. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: At the top it says "HRC Split," and then gives a list of addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, sir, when this letter was written, who was "HRC Split"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ambassador Beaussou.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you again tell us the list of addressees, and again because you're the first witness from ECMM, can you explain to us who these addressees are and what the initials stand for.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The report is issued to headquarters in Zagreb, specifically for the following addressees: The Deputy Head of Mission political, the Deputy Head of Mission operational, the chief operating officer, and with copies to the EC liaison officer with UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, to the coordination centre in Grude, and to the coordination centres in Zenica and the team in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could -- could you please explain to us what the purpose of this document was.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The report appears to be an account of the meeting between the ambassador and a number of senior officials in Mostar in connection with the HVO ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to the second page of this document, please. Do you see the second page, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the paragraph that was carried over from the previous page in the sense of being number 2. If you see the (c). Do you see --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- right above paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you in any way briefed on what is reported in paragraph (c) of page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- that is in line with what Ray Lane reported to me after his meetings in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you, sir, and that -- we're done with that document for the moment. Let me ask you, Mr. Beese, what happened on or about the 20th of January, 1993, with respect to the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: As far as we could observe, the ultimatum was not seen through, and therefore there was no evident change in status between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are there any other events, Mr. Beese, in January, 1993, that stick out in your mind with respect to the situation that you were monitoring based out of Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: There were concerns for the flow of aid from the coast to Central Bosnia. There were changes in the terms required of the aid convoys by the HVO minister for humanitarian affairs, which made it more difficult for aid to flow freely. As far as we could tell, there was intervention in the free flow of aid through the diversion of trucks from Metkovic to Ljubuski where they would be processed, which meant examining the cargos in detail, stripping off what was not required or was not considered to be emergency foodstuffs before the trucks were allowed on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now like to turn your attention, if you would, to February, 1993, and the first few days of February, 1993. Do you recall any of the specific missions that you were tasked with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question with respect to this document. This document, did you have it -- did you read it at the time, or was it Mr. Lane who spoke to you about it? Did you see it with your own eyes? Did you read it yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just based on that, I just want to make sure that we have a procedure in place so I don't have to be objecting too much. Documents that the gentleman did not generate, I don't have a problem in him identifying them as being ECMM documents, but commenting as to the content within the document, if he did not generate that particular document, I would object to. It's a standing objection for all documents to come. Obviously he can talk about observations, perceptions that he generated, you know, at the time. I don't have a problem about that. And this was an issue, by the way, in the previous case where the gentleman testified, so it's nothing novel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, just for the record, I note at page 60, lines 4 and 5, with respect to that paragraph that was shown to the witness, the witness indicated that that paragraph is in line with what Ray Lane reported to him after the meetings in Mostar. So again this is not simply where we're asking him to comment on the contents of documents without him having independent knowledge or an independent basis for that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which is why I do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought it was proper. I thought it was very proper of Mr. Mundis, and I commend him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me again turn your attention, sir, to the first few days of February, 1993, and ask you if you recall any specific missions that you were tasked with as part of your ECMM duties in the first few days or first week of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I recall on the 6th of February being asked by Ray Lane to respond to a request from the United Nations Military Observers in Medjugorje to attend their office without delay. This was in response to a matter that had been reported to the UNMO centre in Medjugorje by their counterpart team in Trebinje to the east of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Beese, what was the subject matter of this request from the UNMOs in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The UNMOs in Medjugorje had been informed by UNMOs in Trebinje that refugees, if one wishes to call them that, had come through the lines at Stolac the previous evening after abduction in Mostar by persons unknown. They had been abducted, taken to the front line at Stolac, pushed across the front line towards the Serbian lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was your specific tasking with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: In Medjugorje, the senior UNMO, Major Paul Ronksley from Canada, briefed myself, Ray Lane, and Joran, the senior UNHCR protection officer in the region, on the material that he'd been advised of, as much as he knew, and we determined how best to respond this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps, if any, did you take in terms of, as you put it, responding to this issue?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane and Paul Ronksley determined to move to Mostar to discuss the matter with the officials there, and in particular Mr. Prlic, whilst I and colleagues moved to Stolac to examine a survivor of the incident in the Stolac hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us this examination that took place in the Stolac hospital.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I met with a woman in her 50s who had been injured by shrapnel and bullet the previous evening. She was in a hospital bed. She was able to talk. And I was accompanied by United Nations Military Observers, Spanish officers from the UNPROFOR battalion at Medjugorje, UNHCR representatives, and HVO representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did this woman tell you when you met with her?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: She recounted how the previous evening she and some 14 other civilians had been taken forcibly from their flats in the Avenue Ante Zuanica in central Mostar. They had been placed in the back of a panel van, driven to Stolac. At the time they were not aware of where they were. It was dark. They were in the back of a van. They were told to get out of the van, and they were told to walk down a road. They understood at that moment that they were close to the front line at Stolac. Some of the women were not accompanied by their husbands who had been elsewhere at the time of the abduction, and refused to cross the front line without their husbands. They had then been shouted at by the abductors, and because of their refusal to move east, grenades were thrown at them together with rifle fire. One woman had been killed by this fire. The injured woman had managed to run away, to cross a river, and to reach some form of sanctuary offered by people on the other side in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, you told us that some of the women were not accompanied by their husbands. Do you know if other people -- other women were accompanied by their husbands?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes, there were. The 14 people abducted were of mixed nationality, including Serb and Muslim, men and women, old and young.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you meet with this woman in Stolac at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour with the woman before moving on to the mortuary to examine the dead woman whose body had been recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how long in total did you remain in Stolac on this day?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Probably an hour and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, where did you go after you were at the hospital and morgue in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I returned through Medjugorje to meet up with Ray Lane and to move to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps, if any, did you subsequently take with respect this incident in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We lodged a complaint with the HVO and specifically with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, when you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ray Lane and myself, but supported by the UNMOs and the protection officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this occasion, Mr. Beese, did you personally meet with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: That would be the 6th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Trial Chamber what was discussed at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The -- the EC and UN lodged a complaint that this had happened. It was understood to have happened in central Mostar. We had visited the flats. The flats were occupied by a number of senior officials, and at the base of the flats was an HVO military police post. We considered that it would not be difficult for the HVO to find out who the abductors were, to investigate the matter, and to report to us. We also asked for assurances that people in Mostar generally should be able to live there safely and not fear for similar abduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, let me ask you a couple of follow-on questions from that answer. You testified the flats were occupied by a number of senior officials. Do you know who these officials were?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I understood senior HVO officials. The only one that was named to me was Petar Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Beese, did you personally visit the flats?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once this information was conveyed to Mr. Prlic, what response, if any, were you given by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic committed to investigate the matter and in due course to issue us with a report of his findings, and he offered the safe return of the abductees and a guarantee of their safety afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, were you in fact in due course presented with a report of Mr. Prlic's findings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On any other occasion did this topic -- again was this topic discussed with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. Several weeks later I asked for a report, I believe of Mr. Prlic, certainly of Mr. Zoric [phoen]. I did not receive ever a report nor any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, the transcript indicates Mr. Zoric. Can you please tell us who you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: To Valentin Coric, who was the head of the military police for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you spell his name?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: C-o-r-i-c. I apologise if I've not pronounced it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown document P 01459. Mr. President, this document was provided to the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 70, so we would ask that this document not be made available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you want to put it on the overhead? We won't focus the camera on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the answer from lines 8 through 10 disappear off the screen, I believe that the transcript contains an error, and I would ask the witness if he could read that answer and make any clarifications or corrections in the event the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, line 11 spells Mr. Coric with a Z when it would be appropriate to have a C, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'm actually referring to the answer immediately above that line.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The same again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could read that entire answer, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. "Several weeks later, I asked for a report, I believe of Mr. Prlic, certainly of Mr. Zoric." Zoric should be spelt with a C. "I did not --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: "I did not receive a report. I never did receive a report or an explanation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So again so that we're clear, did you or did you not receive a report or explanation from the HVO authorities, Mr. Prlic, or Mr. Coric, concerning this incident in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'd now ask if you have P 01459 visible on the screen in front of you, if you could take a look at that document. Can you see this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It appears to be a summary -- summary report from Zagreb, the headquarters ECMM in Zagreb to a -- perhaps a common list of addressees that would be understood by the word "COREU," "Correspondence European Union." That to be to the foreign ministers, to the presidency, and to the peace talks in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, because many of these abbreviations are new to the Trial Chamber perhaps, the first line of this document, can you tell us what that says. I'm not referring to the DK number but the first line of the text.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It is from COP COREU, which is -- I'm not familiar with that particular term having not operated in the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please go to page 2 of this document, and specifically the third full paragraph of that document, the one beginning "In Mostar ..."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: "In Mostar the head of regional centre Split met with Mr. Prlic, president of the HVO, and voiced his disquiet at the abduction of 14 Serbs from Mostar Stolac area and their dispatch across the front line. Mr. Prlic stated that the inquiry into the incident has now -- was now being conducted by the civilian authorities along with the military police. He asked CC Grude to inform those abducted that they had his guarantee of protection if they wished to return to Mostar." Now, Mr. Beese, were you aware or in attendance of a meeting that HRC Split had with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does this paragraph reflect the meeting that you attended, your recollection of what occurred at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask, Mr. Beese, if you could discuss with us a little bit about subsequent events in early to mid-February, 1993. What were your primary taskings after these people were abducted and taken to the front lines in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Our principal concern at that time was the outbreak of violence north of Mostar, and in particular in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And under which coordination centre was Gornji Vakuf at that point in time, early --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, a moment ago you told us that when you were in Stolac, you had a meeting with the lady, 50 years old, and she told you what had happened, and then you said that, because the Prosecutor moved on, that you were in the mortuary to see the woman who had been killed, whereas in the paragraph that we've just shown you, and you said that the 14 individuals were mixed, but in that particular paragraph, you speak about 14 Serbs and there's no mention of people who were killed or injured. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't account for that. Certainly the abduction of 14 would appear to be correct. My understanding is that they were of mixed religion or background, and I cannot account for the lack of comment on the death or injuries inflicted upon the abductees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said that you went to see the body of the person who was killed. Did you see the body of the lady who was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Beese, you mentioned that your principal concern - and this is on lines 4 and 5, page 69 - was the outbreak of violence north of Mostar, and in particular in Gornji Vakuf. In early to mid-February, 1993, Gornji Vakuf was located in which coordination centre's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf was not in any particular area of responsibility. The responsibilities of CC Grude in the south were to monitor the territory principally up to Jablanica and no further. Further north, the people responding to CC Zenica were working down along the Lasva Valley in Vitez and Busovaca. At the time, there was no presence with the ECMM in the area between Jablanica and the Lasva Valley. So Gornji Vakuf did not have a dedicated EC presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Beese, from the period you first arrived in Siroki Brijeg on or about the 9th of January, 1993, until early to mid-February, 1993, were you aware of the conditions or situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that there was some conflict there, but I was not aware of all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Beese, when you were sent to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I travelled north to Gornji Vakuf on the 13th of February, to assist with the operation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long on this occasion in total did you remain in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I would have spent a day in Gornji Vakuf and travelled back I believe that evening, but I was to spend the next several weeks in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, what you observed upon first arriving in Gornji Vakuf on the 13th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I travelled north from Mostar with Ray Lane and officials from the HVO and the armija, in particular General Petkovic of the HVO and Arif Pasalic of the armija. We arrived at the Makljen checkpoint, which is a high feature overlooking Gornji Vakuf, travelled down to the Karamustava checkpoint at the bottom of the hill, where we linked up with a team that had joined us from Split, including Ambassador Beaussou. We then entered Gornji Vakuf along the normal road. It was evident to us from dead animals - that's livestock, cattle, domestic animals, dogs - dead in the fields and beside the streets, and from the number of damaged properties, that there had been conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Beese, that you were travelling with Ray Lane and officials from the armija and the HVO. How many vehicles were in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for making this trip to Gornji Vakuf on the 13th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Ambassador Beaussou and Ray Lane had visited Gornji Vakuf in the days beforehand and spoken with senior officials - I believe Mr. Prlic - with whom they had agreed that a cease-fire was necessary and that the parties should meet in Gornji Vakuf to arrange a cease-fire and ultimately a disengagement of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, did you personally or were you personally involved in these cease-fire negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. I attended them throughout from that day forward until the eventual cease-fire and disengagement on the 18th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber how those negotiations were carried out.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The parties to the talks assembled in the former industrial facility that was occupied by a company of British troops with UNPROFOR. We used that as the base for discussion. We used one room in particular where Ray Lane, myself, and officials from UNPROFOR would chair a meeting between the two parties to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe, Mr. Beese, the atmosphere during these negotiations between the parties to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The talks on the first day - that is the 13th - involved General Petkovic and General Pasalic agreeing that a cease-fire was necessary, agreeing that a disengagement of forces was necessary. Subsequent days involved a meeting of local commanders, in particular the HVO Colonel Zeljko Siljeg and his armija counterparts, as we worked towards a detailed cease-fire and withdrawal. It is not easy to disengage troops, and therefore we had to have a detailed manoeuvre with specific timings and actions. It took some days to come to agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, if you recall, in February, 1993, what were the weather conditions like in the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Cold and progressively colder until it began to snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long in total did these negotiation sessions last?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Every day until the 18th when the cease-fire was implemented first thing in the morning and the disengagement took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us, sir, on lines 12 through 15 that the first day of the talks involved Generals Petkovic and Mr. Pasalic. Did they remain there after that first day?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: No. They handed their responsibility over, having made the decision and issued the orders that talks should continue, to finalise the arrangements to their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there any difficulties encountered in hammering out the final details of this cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. It was a protracted affair. Progress was very slow. Obstructions were placed in the way. Perhaps unavoidably in some cases. The arrival of troops from the Jajce area, both HVO and armija, complicated the withdrawal process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate, Mr. Beese, on obstructions that were placed in the way, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The two -- the two parties had legitimate concerns for significant sized units moving through their zones. If, for instance, armija troops were to disperse to Central Bosnia, they had to pass through territory commanded further north by the HVO Colonel Blaskic. Likewise, HVO forces moving back from the Jajce area had to move through armija positions towards Prozor. It might have been straightforward and relatively easy to agree to the details of those movements, but I believe the process was used to obstruct and delay the outcome and eventual withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And were both parties being obstructive?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: To my understanding and my knowledge, only the HVO were obstructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly about the process of disengagement following the signature of the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The cease-fire would have come into effect at first light on the 18th of February. A number of monitoring teams, not only ourselves but reinforcements from Tomislavgrad and elsewhere, along with UNPROFOR units, were to escort or accompany HVO and armija units as they disengaged, and to observe the cease-fire. A team such as mine included a commissioner, which is a representative, one of the HVO, and one of the armija. So to provide a degree of mutual confidence in the -- the quiet and unobstructed withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the disengagement process, Mr. Beese, where were you? Where did you go, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: My first task was to move to Drimci [phoen], a small village to the south-east of Gornji Vakuf, and to confirm with both commissioners that HVO forces from that area had departed that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And upon your arrival in Zdrimci, can you tell us what you observed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I had not visited the village before. I found it extremely quiet, and I noticed that the Muslim quarter as I knew it or understood it to be, to be completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the rest of the village?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: There were houses that were intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you remain in Zdrimci on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Less than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the weather conditions like?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We had about 20 to 30 centimetres of snow on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity, sir, to visit any of the other areas or any of the other villages in the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I visited the villages of Hrasnica and Grnica. May I apologise here if my pronunciation is not correct for the purpose of transcribing, I'm happy to help to correct it. I also visited the villages to the west of Gornji Vakuf, to the west of the Podavi ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you recall approximately when you left the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: After the cease-fire, the talks continued for a further few days as we endeavoured to address issues of reconstruction. I stayed there for another day or so. I think, on the -- or I believe my account would give me a correct timing and date, but I moved out on the evening of the 18th to Siroki Brijeg, to return a few days later to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me again ask, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher if the document P 01459 could again be shown to the witness, and I would ask that we go to page 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that is happening, if I could draw the attention of the Court to the transcript on page 74, the end of page 74, line 25, the witness was asked a question, "Approximately how long did you remain in Zdrimci on this occasion?" I think his answer, which is omitted from the record, was "Less 10 minutes." Your Honour, if the witness agrees, perhaps the record could be corrected to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I also note there seems to be -- the following question has been omitted which was "What were the weather conditions? " and that answer is reflected in the transcript, there so we seem to be missing an answer and a question at that point in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, the spelling of the villages is also, I believe, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Zdrimci is with a Z at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Those issues will be taken care of when the transcribers review the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me again ask if we could go to the second page of P 01459, and again, Mr. President, I'd ask that this not be broadcast outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, if you could take a look at the paragraph that begins "HRC Split ..." and simply read that to yourself and I'll then ask you a question about that. Mr. Beese, does that description in P 01459 accurately reflect your recollection of the events as described in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The first part to do with a meeting on the 13th of February is correct, but in practice the cease-fire and disengagement did not take place until the 18th. It says here the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese. You told us, sir, that among the -- the people who went with you were these two commissioners. Do you recall who the commissioners were that travelled with you in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Not by name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now ask that the witness be shown a photograph P 09137. And again, Mr. President, this is a Rule 70 document; I believe it needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you see that photograph, Mr. Beese? Not yet.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: No. I can now see the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this photograph depicts.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The photograph is of the room used for meetings between the parties in the UNPROFOR base in Gornji Vakuf. At the head of the table is the chairman of the moment, Mr. Ray Lane. To his left, standing, is myself. And we are surrounded by the local representatives of the two parties, which suggests to me that this would be later in the process, probably some weeks later, perhaps even towards mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese. I'd now like to turn your attention to the period after you left Gornji Vakuf. Do you recall what your primary missions or taskings were in the period beginning in late February into early March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The focus of attention for us shifted from Gornji Vakuf to Prozor where we continued to hold discussions between the HVO and the armija on matters of mutual interest and tension. There were concerns for the release of prisoners who had not yet been released in Gornji Vakuf, for the release of prisoners who had not been released from Prozor, and for the tension in the hills to the north-east of Prozor, particularly in the villages of Here, Kute and Scipe, where refugees were living after their expulsion from Prozor in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, do you recall any meetings that you attended concerning the events in Prozor; any meetings actually in Prozor itself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I held meetings on a number of occasions with the representatives of the HVO and armija, and in particular Colonel Zeljko Siljeg for the HVO, and Amir Bijedic for the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the substantive matters that were discussed in these meetings particularly with Mr. -- or Colonel Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Three matters of concern to me come to mind, in particular his reluctance to release prisoners. It was brought to his attention on a number of occasions that there were, say, a number of prisoners held captive by him and he would variously deny either having prisoners or then agree to a date for their release and fail to meet the date. That was one issue. The second issue concerned the population of Prozor and our belief that there should be some Muslim representation in Prozor. Colonel Siljeg appeared happy to have representation but the Muslim officials did not believe that there was sufficient security in Prozor to enable them to return. And the third issue was the continued pressure directed at the three villages to the east by the HVO, which amounted to a continuation of the conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the specific issues that were discussed concerning the three villages? And again for the record, if you could please tell us which three villages you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The three villages are Here, Kute, and Scipe, which lie some five, six kilometres to the north-east of Prozor on high ground. They had no freedom of movement, they believe, back towards Prozor, and they were effectively cut off. They were also subject to harassing fire from artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were the people that were living in these three villages, Here, Kute, and Scipe?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: They were armija men who had withdrawn from Gornji Vakuf and from Prozor in late 1992, and a significant number of refugees who had lived previously in Prozor, as well as the villagers. There were very few Croats living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you testified, sir, on lines 19 and 20 on page 78, "They were also subject to harassing fire from artillery and mortars." Which force or forces were conducting the harassing fire from artillery and mortars that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall your specific discussions with Colonel Siljeg concerning these three villages?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I raised the matter of -- of harassing fire. I didn't receive a satisfactory response. I was given an explanation of his view of the overall dynamics in the region, and that was that he represented the West in its confrontation with the East. And by that he meant the front line, if you wish, between Christian West and Muslim East.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specific things he told you about this topic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: He explained to me that -- that the matter in -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not dissimilar to circumstances elsewhere in Armenia, Georgia, other parts of Eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you engage Colonel Siljeg in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Not particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was that the first time this subject area had been raised with you during the time you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, after leaving -- let me ask you this: When did you leave the Prozor area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I worked in and around Prozor for some weeks. I would return to Siroki Brijeg, conduct other -- other business, and periodically, say once a week, return to Prozor for further talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, are we talking about the time period in February and March, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- or March, April? What time period?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Late February, early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what were the -- what was the route, the transportation route that you used to travel from Siroki Brijeg to Prozor in late February, early March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I had two options only available to me, and they were the same two options available to anyone else in the region, and that was travelling from Siroki Brijeg to the west through Tomislavgrad over what was known as the Road of Salvation to Prozor, or through Mostar north to Jablanica and north-west to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- what were the conditions like on the road through Mostar north to Jablanica and north-west to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The route from Mostar north to Jablanica is a river valley formed by the Neretva. It's very narrow. It had HVO checkpoints along it almost the entire way to the outskirts of Jablanica. The road was then relatively clear, though there were roadblocks with community police between Jablanica and Prozor. If one went around the other way, the route was entirely clear to Prozor. There were no checkpoints particularly on the road other than one on the Road of Salvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, on line 22 of page 80, you said "... there were roadblocks with community police ..." What community are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Where there were -- were communities, Muslim or Croat, they may have their own armed guards on checkpoints. It was not possible to determine whether they were necessarily official or not. If it was an HVO post, it nearly always had the Croatian flag flying above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these weekly trips to Prozor during this time period, late February, early March, 1993, what were the other issues that you were particularly involved with monitoring?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Continuing tension in Mostar and the need to continue talks with Arif Pasalic and his HVO counterparts, as well as the exchange of people across front lines between HVO territory and Bosnian Serb territory; general discussions with -- with community leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about -- you mentioned continuing tension in Mostar. Can you tell us what the situation was like by this point in time, and again I'm talking late February, early March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Increasing tension, increasing restrictions on movement, I think increasing division between the two communities. They no longer mixed the same way. Muslims living on the west bank felt increasingly uncomfortable. They would be arrested on relatively small charges, detained, and possibly evicted from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, sir, was there any signs of open armed conflict in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Not in Mostar itself, I don't believe. Serb shelling continued randomly at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about humanitarian aid or relief aid reaching the city of Mostar in this time period? Were you aware of -- of any humanitarian aid reaching the city at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Certainly the aid route from the coast to Central Bosnia was increasingly drying. The formalities required of the drivers coming down from Central Bosnia to collect aid were increasing such that more and more trucks came south not to return to the centre again. That produced a degree of desperation in Central Bosnia which began to lack foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain, sir, what you meant by trucks coming south not to return to the centre again?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Trucks belonging to the local authorities and private individuals in Central Bosnia would travel south to collect aid from the port at Ploce. They would then return, passing through the border checkpoint between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina at Metkovic, at which point they were frequently diverted to Ljubuski, a place that became known to us as the Ljubuski Triangle. Trucks and cargos went into it and didn't seem to come out of it. It became a large truck park. Drivers were detained, loads searched, matters that were not -- materials that were not essentially humanitarian - I give an example of coffee - were taken off the trucks. Some trucks allowed to continue, but the need to obtain more passes, prove this, do the other, produced a bureaucratic mechanism that made it almost impossible for the trucks to return to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the effect of this on the centre, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was not familiar with conditions in the centre at that time. One was simply aware that, mathematically, Central Bosnia would one day run out of trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This would be an appropriate place for the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue the hearing. Before I give you the floor, Mr. Mundis, I'd just like to make something clear concerning the documents. You explained to us that there was a first batch that you were going to present to the witness, and you've started that already. Then there's a second batch that I have in front of me, and as I say, it's at least half a metre thick. And I took a look at these documents this morning and noted the following fact: The 3/5th or 4/5th of the documents are posterior, or rather, come after the departure of the witness from Bosnia-Herzegovina. He left on the 21st of July, 1993, and we have documents here dating to August, September, November, December, 1993, and some documents date to 1994, which he could not have known about, of course. So therefore he cannot have knowledge of the documents because he left. Secondly, there are documents during the period that the witness was there, so we could -- well, he could have known about them or not. Now, you should address these documents and just mention the documents that the witness knew of directly or indirectly and then the documents that the witness could not have had any knowledge of, so you'll have to introduce those through another witness. The documents must be shown to the witness at any rate, and we hope the relevancy has been established, and that the witness knows about -- has knowledge of the documents himself or has heard about them. Otherwise, they won't be able to be introduced through this witness. So all this is, I think, clear now. Please continue the examination-in-chief from where we left off, those famous 40 documents. Now, as far as the other documents are concerned, for tomorrow you'll have to make a selection, because certain documents cannot be introduced because the witness left the area in July. So a document dated October, 1993, is one that he has no knowledge of and therefore cannot be introduced through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe we might return to this issue perhaps later this afternoon or tomorrow morning when we get to that point. But for now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- simply to save time and move forward, I would propose that we set that issue aside for the moment and we will undoubtedly return to it later, perhaps in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, immediately before lunch, as reflected on page 82, line 16, of the transcript, you made reference to an area that you told us came to be known as the Ljubuski Triangle. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which force or forces controlled the Ljubuski Triangle?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The controlling force was from the Vojna Policija; that is the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would now like to turn to the period of April, 1993. Can you tell us, sir, what were the primary focus -- or what was the primary focus of your monitoring work in April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I had two priorities: The first was to continue to monitor the confrontation around Prozor and north of Jablanica between HVO and armija forces, which was a continuing concern. The second was the interest shown by HVO authorities in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and the need to begin to consider how, if it was agreed, it might be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me first -- or tell us first a little bit about the work monitoring the confrontation around Prozor and north of Jablanica in this period April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We continued to be aware that there was armed confrontation, that the harassment of Here, Kute, and Scipe continued. From around the 24th of February, 1993, we were aware also that there was manoeuvering north of Lake Jablanicko in the region known as Klis, and most particularly around the villages of Kostajnica held by the HVO and Pasovici held by the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, if I could just stop you there before you continue so this doesn't disappear off the page, on page 85, lines 2 and 3, there was reference to the military police as being the controlling force in Ljubuski. Military police of what military organisation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The Vojna Policija were a department of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry for that interruption. I wanted to clear that up before it disappeared. Can you continue, please, with the efforts in April, 1993, in the Jablanica area.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We were aware at that stage probably for the first time that attempts were being made to secure routes from Herzegovina to Central Bosnia for use by the HVO. And the control of the limited routes became something of considerable importance and increasing importance as the weeks went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, what was the relationship between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Herzegovina was, if you like, the undisputed power base of the HVO. The population of the area west of the Neretva and south-west of Mostar, including the towns of Grude, Siroki Brijeg, Ljubuski, Capljina, Citluk, Posusje, Tomislavgrad, and Livno were almost entirely Croat and dominated by the HVO. The area north of Mostar, the Dreznica valley, Jablanica, Konjic, and Klis, that is between Lake Jablanicko and the Lasva Valley were controlled primarily by the armija. North of that in the Lasva Valley were a string of communities, including Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, and Novi Travnik that were controlled by HVO again with significant Croat populations. Those populations were armed, there was conflict between them and their neighbours along the Lasva Valley, and it appeared to us that they were endeavouring to control the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, Mr. Beese, it appeared to you that "they were endeavouring to control the Lasva Valley," what or to whom does the word "they" apply?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And from where were they attempting to control the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: From their bases in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you know, what was the relationship between the bases in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak and those areas controlled by the HVO in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: To broaden the subject, it appeared to us that the HVO in Mostar sought to consolidate power in Herzegovina but sought control of the economic facilities along the Neretva Valley, the water resources, hydroelectric plants and the like, and to do that they had to control the ground immediately beyond it. They also had to reinforce their colleagues in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: By what means were they attempting to reinforce their colleagues in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: There was a need to resupply them. I'm confident they had communication between the various communities, but they needed to move up fuel, munitions, and other war materiel necessary to exercise control of the critical Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And based on your observations, were they successful in doing that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: No, not entirely. In fact, each attempt to open a new route was frustrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about these attempts to open new routes that you were familiar with from your observation and monitoring work.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Before my arrival in theatre, the town of Jajce had been lost to Serb forces. The town of Jajce and Donji Vakuf to its south-east provided a -- an effective route for heavy transport from the south to Central Bosnia and was therefore suitable for resupply. That route had been lost when Jajce fell, and the significance of that was brought to my attention when a number of people remarked how furious the Croats had been that the Muslims appeared to have collapsed at Jajce and permitted its fall. That was the best route from the south to the north in terms of road surface. It became apparent to me from circumstances and discussions that the attack on Gornji Vakuf had been designed to secure the second route from Prozor north through Gornji Vakuf to Novi Travnik and into Central Bosnia. Lack of control of Gornji Vakuf meant lack of control of resupply. From what we've already discussed today, the ongoing tension east of Prozor, it appeared to me that the Croats were attempting to use forestry haul roads, perhaps improved by engineers, to break out north-east from Prozor towards Fojnica and again link up. That was frustrated by the continuing resistance of the three villages Here, Kute, and Scipe. The outbreak of violence in Kostajnica appeared to be an attempt to destabilise the Klis region and perhaps force a route up from Kostajnica across Klis to Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Beese, whether you were aware of command and control links between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia with respect to HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: It was apparent, again through discussion, visits, that the HVO command in Mostar was aware of circumstances in Central Bosnia on an hourly basis, which presumably would have been facilitated by radio. There was no other means of managing those communications. There were not effective road communications, it was not possible for people to easily physically travel between Central Bosnia and Mostar. The telephone lines were not operational, and therefore given that the HVO in Mostar always appeared to know what was going on, one can only assume that they had radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return, sir, to discussions about your involvement in terms of monitoring the situation in and around Jablanica in April, 1993. Can you tell us, sir, at that point in time where you were and what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: In late March and early April, 1993, I was involved with discussions between the HVO and, through Arif Pasalic, the Presidency in Sarajevo on the need to consider ways to implement the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, but while I was talking with the HVO about agendas for this meeting and the peaceful way forward, I was aware that increasing pressure was brought to bear on the Klis region and Jablanica. Jablanica is a key point in the region, not only because it is a focal point for road communications but also has control of the water sources derived from Lake Ramsko outside Prozor to Mostar in the south. Therefore, if there was to be control of the water resources and hydroelectric facilities, Jablanica had to be taken control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interject here for one second. I understand that the gentleman has a military background. I understand that he was an observer. He told us the purposes for which he was observing. We now seem to be going into areas which would indicate that perhaps he's testifying as an expert, as it were. If that is the case, I would like to know whether he's been qualified as an expert, if he's rendering opinions as an expert, or are these merely his -- his observations as a layperson, which means that when it comes time to weighing his testimony, it would have less weight to be given to it since he's a layperson as opposed to being an expert. So I mention this because I think we're going into an area where he is testifying into matters that might appear to require some sort of an expertise and therefore he needs to be qualified as an expert if indeed he is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, with respect to the remarks made by Defence counsel, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, clearly -- clearly, Mr. President, the witness has told us earlier about his experience, the skills that he had obtained, the purpose of his work, how his work was undertaken, and given the totality of the circumstances, including briefings and consultation with his colleagues, he's certainly qualified to reach these types of conclusions with respect to things he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, if Mr. -- Mr. Mundis, if you had presented a report, we would -- we would have been able to see the sense of the remarks differently, and I would like to make things quite clear. Mr. Beese, tell us, please, you spoke at length about the lake from which the water was derived for certain localities, and you explained why it was important for the HVO to have control of that water source. So that is actually an assessment that ought to be made by an expert witness. The question now is, did you include those types of comments in the reports you sent out to the headquarters of the ECMM? Did you include in your reports things like that? Did you describe a lake XY and say that the lake was important from the military point of view because it was a water supply for certain settlements or things like that? So was that part of your mission, to observe matters of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was. There were others in the region who were able to report, for instance, how many shells had landed in a particular place on a particular day. That itself was not a difficult task. It was much more important for some of us to understand why they landed where they landed at and what that meant, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So you're telling us that when you're answering the questions put to you by the Prosecution, the answers that you are giving us are personal observations that you saw on the ground, and those observations you mention in the reports, and you send them out to the people that sent you on the mission. Is that how I am to understand your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have to say one thing. If you look earlier, he talked about the importance of the communications, the roads. Then he talked about the water. And then he was -- he was asked a question by Mr. Mundis -- or Mr. Mundis made a comment that the gentleman is qualified to render these sorts of opinions. These are, in my -- in my humble opinion, what he's using the gentleman for and what the gentleman seems to be alluding to is that he is a military expert and therefore his opinions are of -- of that nature. If that is indeed the case, then obviously under the Rules he should have been qualified as an expert, he should have prepared a report, and we should have been able to at least anticipate that he would be coming in as an expert, but that does not seem to be the case. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the witness was recruited by the Foreign Office, he explained to us that he had an interview and that when he was recruited, he was recruited because of his military past experience. He had been to the military academy of Sandhurst, and if somebody is an officer, then somebody can address matters of communication and routes. He can stress the strategic importance. You don't have to be an expert for that. And we can say that a certain road is of strategic importance. So I don't see where the problem is on that score. But let's stop there. Mr. Mundis, continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd ask that the witness now be shown the document marked P 01911.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, can you see a document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: This is a report written for the purpose of better understanding the crisis in Jablanica as viewed by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to renew my objection, Your Honour, just for the record, for the sake of the record, because if I just look at it, it says "Political and military analysis." So now we're into the area where the gentleman is going to be testifying about a document generated as a military expert. So I just renew my objection so at least we're clear that I'm not waiving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think you are well aware, as we all are, that there are flowing limits between a witness and an expert and to a large extent our witness has spoken about his own experience, and I think it's quite correct that this includes assessments he has made. That is also a fact the witness can talk about as something which he has personally witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree, Your Honour. My question has to go to weight, because otherwise, if he's deemed an expert, the Trial Chamber may give his testimony more weight than a layperson. That was my concern. So that's why I wanted a designation. Is he testifying as an expert or merely giving his observation as a lay witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, the Prosecution position would certainly be that there are shades of witnesses, as alluded to by Judge Trechsel, including there are some people who might be considered lay witnesses who have a certain degree of knowledge and experience that might give their testimony greater weight than if you simply took cab drivers off the street and sent them down to Bosnia as -- as monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Beese, can you tell us for what purpose this report P 01911 was drafted?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The purpose was to present the situation as we saw it in the Jablanica and Klis area quite clearly to our superiors in Split and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the basis, or how did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was privileged to have a fairly unique degree of access to people, access to places. I had dozens of discussions and field visits and the time devoted to understand what was happening around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please -- I'd ask with the assistance of Mr. Registrar that the section marked 2, "Regional Importance," at the bottom of this document be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Beese, if you can read it on the screen, could you just take a quick look to yourself, read it to yourself, the bottom part of this document under heading 2, "Regional Importance."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when this report was written, how you came about obtaining the information that's in this document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: My visits to discussions in and understanding of the situation around Prozor, Jablanica, and Konjic gave me cause to analyse the reasons for certain actions. It would have been very easy, given the HVO's declared interest in peace, to have left peace in place. This was not in fact the case. Therefore, if there was military manoeuvre in the region, there had to be an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What military manoeuvre in the region are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the need to secure routes, that is the engagements in Gornji Vakuf, then east of Prozor, then in Kostajnica, and the apparent reinforcement of the area south-west of Jablanica by HVO troops moving in from Tomislavgrad to put pressure on Jablanica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go to the second page of this document. Mr. Beese, I'd like to turn your attention to the paragraph or subheading 3, "Political Activity." Who drafted this part of this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon what basis did you write this section of the report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: May I please read it first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The information that's contained in this part of the report, what was the source for that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Reports from monitoring teams, the discussions with the officials of both parties, and travel through the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please turn to page 4 of this document. Now, Mr. Beese, at the top it is indicated under number 6, "Indicators," and I'm wondering if you could tell us a little bit about what you meant by the use of the term "indicators."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: These are some of the contributing factors that have been reviewed and support a view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please read out for us the fourth paragraph of this document, and then I'd like to ask you a question or two about that, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Certainly. "The HVO make regular radio broadcast ultimatums to the Muslim forces in Herceg-Bosna (they never appear written) yet seldom follow up the ultimatums, suggesting that the concept is to provoke Muslims into action that can then be used to justify aggression in the name of defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was the author of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Beese, what was the basis for you writing that sentence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: The discussions with the armija who reported to us that the ultimatums had been delivered. We never received word from the HVO that they had these intentions. That itself is unusual, given a general commitment to peace, and the abstention from any move that may raise tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, by "the abstention from any move that may raise tension"? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: In discussions with HVO authorities, we would hear their commitment to peace and to a working relationship with the Muslim party, but the issue of ultimatums could not be seen to be given in the context of that. They were at odds with statements given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: Because there was no need other than an administrative convenience to bring Muslim forces under control of the HVO. It perhaps made perfect sense as a strategy that they work together in closer cooperation, but there are better ways to bring people within your fold than to deliver ultimatums, particularly if you deliver them through media means rather than through direct negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, during the time period that you were in Bosnia in 1993, on how many occasions were you aware of these ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was aware of at least two that come to mind. The first was the one of 16 January. The second was the 14th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, before we leave this general area about specific locations, if any, that you went to in Jablanica municipality in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I travelled the hills around Here, Kute, and Scipe. I travelled the road frequently from Prozor to Jablanica. I crossed Lake Jablanicko into Kostajnica and Pasovici, and I travelled frequently into Konjic to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time become aware of conflict in the Sovici or Doljani areas?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I became aware from mid-March that tension was rising in the region, and the outbreak of violence in Kostajnica confirmed our concerns. I was later aware of problems in Sovici and Doljani, initially as rumour, that there were problems, that there were expulsions of Muslims by HVO, and the burning of villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you personally ever go to either of those two villages?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: I was denied access, as were my teams and the UNMOs, to that area. We could neither gain entry through Tomislavgrad to the west nor directly from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, with respect to the entry through Tomislavgrad to the West, which force denied entry to Sovici, Doljani?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We had a team based at Tomislavgrad which endeavoured to move from Tomislavgrad north-east towards Sovici and Doljani and was turned back at HVO roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And with respect to attempts to gain entry to those locations from Jablanica, what force denied entry?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE
utterances.text: We made a number attempts.
